caption:
Apple CEO John Ternus says Apple will use AI across its products, but "we don't want to ship AI for AI's sake."
In an interview with WIRED, he pushed back on the idea that Apple has fallen behind: "I really like where we're at."
His goal is AI so built in that people never wonder whether AI did it.

Is Apple smart to take its time on AI, or is it already too late?

Follow @neurafeed.ai for daily AI news.

Source: WIRED via ShiftDelete.Net · Photo: David Swanson/Reuters, 9to5Mac, Apple
threads_text: Apple's new CEO John Ternus says Apple won't "ship AI for AI's sake" and that he really likes where the company stands in AI. His bet is AI so built in you never notice it. Smart patience, or a nice way of saying Apple is behind?

slides.headline: Critics say Apple is losing the AI race. Its new CEO says *he likes where they're at*

site_article.headline: Apple CEO John Ternus says Apple will not ship AI for its own sake
site_article.dek: In an interview with WIRED, the new chief executive rejected the view that Apple trails in AI and said the best AI features are ones users do not notice.
site_article.summary: Apple CEO John Ternus told WIRED that Apple will use AI throughout its products but does not want to ship "AI for AI's sake." He pushed back on outside views that the company has fallen behind in the AI race.
site_article.seo_title: John Ternus: Apple won't ship AI for AI's sake
site_article.seo_description: Apple CEO John Ternus told WIRED that Apple will use AI in its products but will not ship AI for its own sake, and rejected claims it is behind.
site_article.answer_summary: Ternus said Apple will use AI in its products, but only where it makes them better, and that done well, people will not need to know whether AI was involved.

paragraphs.text: Apple chief executive John Ternus said the company will use AI across its products but does not want to ship "AI for AI's sake," in an interview with WIRED's Steven Levy published on October 30, 2026. The conversation took place after Apple's MacBook Pro launch in Los Angeles that week, according to ShiftDelete.Net, which summarized the interview.

Ternus said Apple is "absolutely going to leverage AI" in new products. He framed the question as one of usefulness rather than labels, saying that when Apple gets it right, "people won't have to think about whether it was AI that made this happen." DigitalToday reported that he described the real test as whether Apple makes products people truly like.
Pushing back on the laggard label

Apple has faced repeated claims that it is behind rivals in generative AI, a perception that ShiftDelete.Net tied largely to Siri. Asked about the competing narratives around the company, Ternus said, "Everyone has an opinion. I really like where we're at." DigitalToday, citing TechCrunch's report on the interview, described the remarks as a direct rejection of outside assessments that Apple has fallen behind.

Ternus was also asked whether AI agents could make apps unnecessary and reshape Apple's ecosystem. According to DigitalToday, he said agents could make life much more convenient, while arguing that "the creation of products is a deeply human and personal thing" that Apple loves to do.
A product chief in the top job

Ternus, 51, officially took over as chief executive in early September 2026 after 25 years at Apple. Former CEO Tim Cook is now executive chairman, and Ternus said Cook "is available to help wherever I ask him." Apple's hardware engineering and technology groups have been merged under chip chief Johny Srouji, who reports to Ternus, according to ShiftDelete.Net.

Marketing chief Greg Joswiak and Srouji both described Ternus as a product person, ShiftDelete.Net reported. Asked which chief executives or business books he admires, Ternus said he had not given it much thought and learns most from his colleagues. On regulation, he pointed to security, saying Apple's focus is on keeping products safe and protecting user data. He also said he has not yet met President Donald Trump.

The interview came days after Apple introduced its first touchscreen MacBook Pro. ShiftDelete.Net noted that the return of the glowing Apple logo to the laptop's lid drew the loudest reaction from the audience at the launch event.

The comments suggest Apple under Ternus intends to keep competing on finished products rather than on model announcements or chatbot benchmarks. That approach fits Apple's history, but it also puts more weight on how well AI features actually work inside its devices, since Apple is choosing not to market the technology itself. Siri remains the most visible place where that promise will be judged.
The next test is Siri: how Apple's coming AI updates to its assistant land with users will show whether AI that people do not notice can close the gap critics describe.
